title: At Sinai: A Kingdom of Priests and a Holy Nation
summary: In the third month after leaving Egypt, Israel camps before Mount Sinai. God offers a covenant: he has carried them on eagles' wings, and if they obey him they will be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people agree, spend three days preparing behind a boundary, and on the third day the LORD descends on the mountain in cloud, fire, smoke, earthquake, and the rising blast of the ram's horn.
story: Everything since the burning bush has been heading here. At the bush God told Moses that the sign of his sending would be this: “all of you will worship God on this mountain” (3:12). Now they have arrived. The rescue from Egypt was not the end of the story but the start of a relationship, since God brought Israel out of slavery in order to bring them “to Myself” (verse 4), and at Sinai that relationship takes the form of a covenant. Israel will stay at the mountain from here to Numbers 10, nearly a year, and the law of Exodus 20-40, Leviticus, and Numbers 1-10 is all given in that encampment. The promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his family stands behind verses 5-6. Israel is chosen out of all the nations, but for the sake of a whole earth that belongs to God.
historical:
The location of Mount Sinai is disputed. Christian tradition since at least the fourth century has identified it with Jebel Musa (Arabic for the mountain of Moses) in the granite range of the southern Sinai Peninsula, where the Monastery of Saint Catherine was built under the emperor Justinian in the sixth century. Other proposals include nearby Jebel Serbal, peaks in the northern Sinai closer to Kadesh, and sites in northwestern Arabia, the land of Midian, where some scholars have pointed to volcanic peaks that might fit the fire and smoke of verse 18. Paul's reference to “Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25) is cited in that debate, though the name Arabia was used loosely in his day. No site has been confirmed by archaeology, and the Old Testament shows little interest in the mountain as a place of pilgrimage; the only later figure it sends there is Elijah (1 Kings 19:8).

Verse 1 dates the arrival to the third month after the exodus. Later Jewish tradition connected the giving of the law with the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot, called Pentecost in Greek), which fell fifty days after Passover, and the festival came to celebrate the gift of the Torah as well as the wheat harvest.
cultural:
Approaching a god in the ancient world required preparation, and Israel's is simple: wash clothes, stay behind a boundary, and abstain from sexual relations for three days. That last instruction does not treat marriage as sinful. In Israel's purity law, intercourse left a couple ritually unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:18), unready for a time to approach the holy, much as contact with a dead body did. The same custom appears when David's men may eat the consecrated bread only because they have kept themselves from women (1 Samuel 21:4-5). Holiness in Israel was not only moral; it also concerned the boundaries of life and death, which had to be kept apart from the presence of the living God.

The phrase “a kingdom of priests” draws on what priests did. A priest stood between God and people, taught God's ways, and brought offerings; Israel as a whole is to stand in that position toward the nations. The word for treasured possession (segullah) was used for a king's personal treasure, as when David gives his own gold and silver for the temple (1 Chronicles 29:3). The ram's horn (shofar) was ancient Israel's trumpet, blown to gather assemblies, sound alarms, and announce a king.
literary: The chapter moves in three steps: the offer of the covenant (verses 1-8), the preparation (verses 9-15), and the descent of God (verses 16-25). The offer in verses 3-6 is a short poem set inside the narrative, and it has the shape of a covenant in miniature: what God has done (verse 4), what he asks (verse 5), and what he promises (verses 5-6). Moses goes up and down the mountain again and again, carrying words between God and the people, which establishes his role as mediator before any law is given. The number three runs through the preparation, and the theophany (a visible appearance of God) gathers every sign of power an ancient reader knew: thunder, lightning, thick cloud, fire, smoke like a furnace, earthquake, and a horn growing louder and louder. Nothing is said about what God looks like. Deuteronomy makes the point explicit: “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12).

outline.t: Israel camps in front of the mountain
The covenant offer: eagles' wings and a kingdom of priests
The people's answer and the promise of the cloud
Three days of consecration and a boundary around the mountain
The LORD descends in fire, smoke, and thunder
A second warning to keep back

doctrines.note: The covenant rests on what God has already done: “You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt” (verse 4). Obedience is Israel's response to rescue, not the price of it. The condition in verse 5 is real, but it is spoken to people who have already been carried on eagles' wings.

God's holiness is a presence so pure that touching the mountain means death. The boundary, the washing, and the waiting teach that a holy God cannot be approached casually. Yet the same God who descends in fire has called the people out to meet him, so holiness here is both danger and invitation.

Israel is chosen out of all the nations, “for the whole earth is Mine” (verse 5). Election is for service. A kingdom of priests exists to bring God near to others, and a holy nation is meant to show the world what the God who rescued it is like.

words.note: Segullah, treasured possession. The word names a king's private treasure (1 Chronicles 29:3; Ecclesiastes 2:8). Every nation belongs to God, but Israel is his in a particular, cherished way. The term returns in Deuteronomy 7:6 and 14:2, and Malachi 3:17 uses it for the faithful who belong to God on the day he acts.

Berit, covenant: a binding relationship sealed by oath, with obligations attached. God has already remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (2:24); now he offers Israel as a people a covenant of its own, which will be sealed with blood in chapter 24. Scholars often compare its shape with ancient treaties in which a history of the great king's kindness came before his requirements.

Qadash, to be holy, or in this form to set apart and consecrate. Moses consecrates the people (verses 10 and 14), the priests must consecrate themselves (verse 22), and the mountain is set apart as holy (verse 23). Holiness in Scripture begins with belonging: what is holy has been set apart for God, and the moral sense follows, since what belongs to him must reflect his character.

christ: The New Testament gives the words of verses 5-6 to the church. Peter writes to believers that they are “a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9), and Revelation says Christ has made his people “a kingdom and priests to serve our God” (Revelation 5:10). Hebrews 12:18-24 sets this chapter beside the new covenant. Christians have not come to a mountain that burns with fire, with darkness and a trumpet blast, but to Mount Zion, to God the Judge of all, and “to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:24). The contrast does not make God less holy; it says the way to him is now opened through Christ. Many readers also notice that the Spirit is given at Pentecost, the festival later tied to Sinai, with a sound from heaven and tongues like fire (Acts 2), though Luke does not draw the connection himself.

hard.q: Why is God so dangerous to approach that even an animal touching the mountain must die?
hard.a: The warnings are severe. Anyone who touches the mountain must be stoned or shot, so that no one touches the offender, and God will break out against those who force their way up. Hebrews recalls the terror of it: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned” (Hebrews 12:20). Modern readers can find this harsh or arbitrary. The text's own logic is that holiness is real and dangerous to whatever is not holy, the way fire is dangerous without being cruel; the rule covers animals because the danger lies in contact, not in guilt. On this reading the boundary is a mercy, since God comes near and tells the people exactly how to survive his nearness. Some interpreters stress that the rules taught reverence at the moment the relationship began, as the deaths of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10) and of Uzzah (2 Samuel 6) later show that God's presence cannot be handled carelessly. Others read the scene as a picture of the distance sin creates, which the rest of Scripture sets out to close. Both agree the barrier is not the last word: in 24:9-11 Israel's elders eat and drink on the mountain in God's presence.

questions: God reminds Israel of what he has already done before he asks anything of them. How does remembering what God has done change the way you hear what he asks?
Israel was chosen out of all the nations for the sake of the whole earth. Where are you tempted to treat God's gifts as privileges to keep rather than a calling to serve others?
The people were warned not to break through to see the LORD. What does reverence look like in a culture that prizes familiarity and ease?
